data: A single independent reviewer from another model family is the sharper choice for improving a draft plan like the vsect maturation plan.

It directly attacks the exact failure modes that turn a good outline into a landing disaster: hidden dependencies, unstated assumptions, and steps that look fine on paper but collapse under execution.

The 43 % 116/116 statistic you cite is about post-landing verification, but the same principle applies upstream—self-reviewers (or same-family reviewers) systematically under-detect structural holes because they share the author’s mental model and confirmation bias.
An outsider from a different substrate forces a fresh pass at the plan’s logic, dependencies, and edge cases without the author’s blind spots.
A council, while useful for final sign-off or hard cases, is the wrong instrument here.
Its native output is a vote or recommendation, which slides into grading language (“looks good,” “approved”) rather than the precise redlines a plan needs to become executable.

The 43 % defect rate you reference shows that even when self-checks are perfect, independent eyes still find problems; a council’s multi-vantage benefit is real, but it arrives at the cost of coordination overhead and the risk that conflicting notes collapse into a binary decision instead of actionable edits.

tool_input.text: For a draft plan like the vsect maturation plan, use one independent reviewer from another model family. Charge that reviewer to return specific changes that would improve the draft: missing steps, wrong dependencies, unstated assumptions, and checks that would not catch a bad landing. Forbid a review that is only a grade. Do not convene a council as the default checker. Escalate to a council only if the reviewer and the author cannot resolve a claimed defect, or if the plan commits irreversible or cross-cutting work. Independence plus a different model family is what breaks the 116-of-116 self-confirmation failure. A council's natural product is a decision, and a decision grades a plan instead of improving it.

data: The meeting wrapped up cleanly on the call-to-order side, but the open-round mechanics left me a bit puzzled.
When the brief said “Move what you would recommend,” all four seats moved at once, yet only one motion actually got the floor.
I assumed the others would become standing intents, but the rules never spelled out that simultaneous moves would compete for the floor or how the winner was chosen.
Fam and I later co-made when our text was identical, but Cost’s and Indept’s near-duplicates sat as standing intents because their wording differed by a few characters.
That felt a little unfair—substance agreed, yet floor assignment hinged on byte-level identity.
The amendment path was also unclear until Fam explained it: debate → maker withdraws → new motion.
I proposed an amendment “for the maker to adopt” without realizing the maker couldn’t amend in place, and I passed once thinking I couldn’t move, which was correct for that round.
Standing intents were helpful, but the “re-affirm by moving it, possibly revised” rule only surfaced when the floor reopened.
